miniProject.title: Deterministic replication and stream-replay simulation over the service log
miniProject.brief: Simulate the service slice replicated and consumed, in one process with logical ticks: a leader and followers with configuration IDs, ownership transfer with fencing, and a consumer group that replays the log into derived state. Drive it through lag, duplicates, a stale read, an ownership change, replay and node loss, then defend the contract with one history it permits and one it rejects.
steps: Write `kv/sim/scheduler.py`: an event loop over integer ticks with a stable insertion-order tie-break and one seeded random source owned by the scheduler. A schedule delivers, delays, drops or duplicates messages, and crashes nodes, which lose volatile state, keep what they persisted and can restart. Every run writes the client history \((\text{process}, \text{operation ID}, \text{object}, \text{input}, \text{invocation tick}, \text{response tick}, \text{result})\) as JSON, and the same seed must give a byte-identical history three times.

Model three replicas of the service log. The leader acknowledges according to a declared mode, after its own `fsync` or after a majority has persisted, and every operation records the configuration ID it used. Reproduce asynchronous-failover loss (the leader acknowledges, dies, and a follower without the write is promoted) and the unit's stale-membership read (write through A, B, C; read through C, D, E before state transfer returns 0). Then show that majority persistence with a membership change that blocks reads in the new configuration until state transfer completes keeps the acknowledged write in the same schedules.

Write `kv/sim/check.py`: a brute-force linearizability checker for one register over small histories that enumerates orders respecting response-before-invocation and treats a timed-out write as possibly applied. It must reject the unit's H1 and the stale-follower read, and accept H2 and the leader-read repair. Add checks for read-your-writes and monotonic reads, and classify every history you produce as linearizable, session consistent only, or neither.

Add a multi-writer mode with last-write-wins on \((\text{timestamp}, \text{node})\) and reproduce the lost update: two concurrent writes converge to one value in both arrival orders, and the other acknowledged write is gone. Write an application merge for a set with removals (tombstoned elements or an observed-remove set) and test the unit's cart case: removed items stay removed, where plain union brings them back.

Partition keys over 12 fixed shards owned by nodes. Move shards 3, 7 and 11 to a new node (three keys move, where remapping \(k \% 3\) to \(k \% 4\) moves nine) and count requests per node under a hot key (90 requests for key 0 give `[93, 4, 4]` over three nodes). Transfer ownership with a fencing token persisted at the log resource with the mutation: a delayed write from the old owner with token 7 is rejected after the resource has seen token 8 and accepted before. Keep both schedules, and the overwrite when the check is removed.

Treat each replica log as a retained partition and write a consumer group that applies records to derived state in SQLite, storing the next offset in the same transaction, one checkpoint per group and partition. Crash it at each boundary (offset before effect, effect before offset, inside and after the transaction) and show only the atomic version matches a sequential oracle; two groups keep independent checkpoints. Mark an external effect (an email stub) as outside the transaction and give it its own idempotency key.

Add event time: records carry `event_at`, the watermark is the maximum seen minus a declared lateness, windows are width-10 tumbling, and late events go to a side output (with lateness 3, the unit's `[2, 12, 4]` gives late `[4]` and watermark 9). Retry a poison record a bounded number of times, then move it to a durable dead-letter table with its offset, reason and replay policy, and mark the window output incomplete. Report offset lag (end offset minus the group's next offset) apart from event-time lateness. Snapshot with the next offset, compact keeping tombstones, kill the consumer node and show snapshot plus suffix equals full replay; then show an expired tombstone bringing back a deleted key.

Run one scenario through lag, a duplicate, a stale read, an ownership change, a replay and a node loss, and write the contract on one page: what an acknowledgement means, which consistency reads get in each mode, the consumer's delivery guarantee and what is excluded. Give one history it permits and one it rejects, each checked by `kv/sim/check.py`. Optionally trace a two-map word count over the log with one failed attempt kept private and a retry checked against a `Counter` oracle (\(a=2\), \(b=2\), \(c=1\); \(a=4\), \(b=3\), \(c=1\) if both attempts publish).
deliverables: `kv/sim/`: scheduler, replicas, fencing, consumer and stream state, with tests that replay every seeded scenario byte for byte.
`kv/sim/check.py` with the linearizability and session checks and their fixtures (H1, H2, stale read, repair).
The scenario histories as JSON and the one-page contract with its permitted and rejected history.
The consumer crash-boundary table and the stream-state tests: late data, dead letters, snapshot plus suffix and tombstone expiry.

rubric.pass: The same seed gives byte-identical histories, and every fault comes from the schedule, not from wall-clock timing.
rubric.strong: A failing scenario found by a random seed is cut down by hand to a short schedule kept as a regression.

rubric.pass: Asynchronous-failover loss and the stale-membership read are reproduced with configuration IDs on every operation, and the repaired mode keeps the acknowledged write.
rubric.strong: The write-up separates quorum intersection, persisted acknowledgements and membership coordination as three distinct requirements.

rubric.pass: The checker rejects H1 and the stale read, accepts H2 and the repair, and treats timed-out writes as possibly applied.
rubric.strong: Every produced history is classified, and one fixture is accepted only because a pending write may have taken effect.

rubric.pass: Fencing rejects the delayed write once the resource has seen the new token, and only the atomic consumer matches the oracle at every crash boundary.
rubric.strong: The dead-letter path and the tombstone-expiry failure each state which completeness claim they change.

rubric.pass: The one-page contract names the acknowledgement meaning, read consistency, delivery guarantee and exclusions, with one permitted and one rejected history.
rubric.strong: Every claim in the contract points to the scenario and test that support it.

miniProject.feedsInto: Capstone service slice: the offset invariant and the deterministic process faults. Dossier: the distributed history with its permitted and rejected cases.
